# Previously on these screens

* The NHANES dataset: welcome to the real deal
* Inspecting, assessing, cleaning data
* Processing and transforming data
* Combining datasets


## There are data types

::: {.fragment}
Some of them, we already encountered - and some of them are... a bit special

::: {.incremental}
* Numbers
* Strings
* Factors
* Dates
* Missing (yep, a missing info can also be/become an information)
:::
:::

::: {.fragment}
We have been working with our `nh_ghb` dataset, let's reload it into our session

```{r}
library("NHANES")
library("dplyr")

# checkpoint from chapter 4
nh_ghb <- readRDS("datasets/nhanes_ghb.RDS")
```
:::

# 1. Factors

## Text vs. categories

Let's have a closer look, with a specific focus on this!

::: {.fragment}
```{r}
#| eval: false
class(nh_ghb$bmi_class)   
unique(nh_ghb$bmi_class)
class(nh_ghb$Diabetes)    
levels(nh_ghb$Diabetes)

unclass(nh_ghb$Diabetes)

table(nh_ghb$bmi_class)
table(nh_ghb$bmi_class, useNA = "always")
```

What order is this? is it meaningful?

<!-- Callback to chapter 3: `case_when()` gave us "heavy, light, medium". Alphabetical, not logical. -->
:::

## Levels have an order

... and it can be related to a meaning

```{r}
#| eval: true
levels(NHANES$Education)
levels(NHANES$AgeDecade)       # Can you spot anything odd in the labels?

table(NHANES$Education)
## or 
NHANES |> 
  count(Education)
```

::: {.fragment}
The "information content" is the same, the behavior/format sometimes is not. Where do you find all this info on functions?
:::

## Set the order yourself

Let's fix the `bmi_class`

::: {.fragment}
```{r}
#| eval: true
nh_ghb <- nh_ghb |>
  mutate(
    bmi_class = factor(bmi_class,
                       levels = c("underweight", "normal", "overweight", "obese"))
  )

levels(nh_ghb$bmi_class)
count(nh_ghb, bmi_class)           # now the table reads in a meaningful order
```
:::

::: {.fragment}
What happened to our `NA`s?

For more factor-centric functions, you can have a look at the `forcats` package (yes, this is an intentional anagram of `factors`).
:::

## Why bother? 

::: {.fragment}
Well, because the order shows up also in plots
:::

::: {.fragment}
```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: false

library("ggplot2")

nh_ghb |>
  # drop_na(bmi_class) |>
  count(bmi_class) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = bmi_class, y = n)) +
  geom_col()
```
:::

# 2. Missing values

## `NA` is "unknown"

::: {.fragment}
It is not zero!
:::

::: {.fragment}
Back to some basics:

```{r}
#| eval: true
x <- c(120, 135, NA, 110)
mean(x)
mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)
is.na(x)
sum(is.na(x))
```
:::

## How much is missing, and where?

This is quite a useful overview (kind of applies to any rectangular data...)

::: {.fragment}
```{r}
#| eval: true
nh_ghb |>
  summarise(across(everything(), ~ sum(is.na(.x)))) |>
  t()
```
:::

::: {.fragment}
What does `t()` do in here?
:::

## Back to blood pressure

How many/much is missing?

```{r}
#| eval: true
sum(is.na(nh_ghb$BPSys1))
mean(is.na(nh_ghb$BPSys1))         # proportion missing
```

::: {.fragment}
*Who is missing? Make a guess before you look.*
:::

## Is it random?

Let's have a look

::: {.fragment}
```{r}
#| eval: true
nh_ghb |>
  mutate(bp_missing = is.na(BPSys1)) |>
  group_by(age_group) |>
  summarise(n = n(), prop_missing = mean(bp_missing))
```
:::

::: {.fragment}
In this case, the info is missing by **design** (children not measured), not by accident. 

You can check it with `range(nh_ghb$Age[!is.na(nh_ghb$BPSys1)])`.
:::

## Three ways to deal with NAs

Run these commands sequentially, and see what comes out

```{r}
#| eval: false
# 1. ignore inside the function
nh_ghb |> 
  summarise(mean_sbp = mean(BPSys1, na.rm = TRUE),
            n = n())

# 2. drop rows with NA in one variable
nh_ghb |> 
  drop_na(BPSys1) |> 
  summarise(mean_sbp = mean(BPSys1), 
            n = n())

# 3. filter explicitly
nh_ghb |> 
  filter(!is.na(BPSys1)) |> 
  summarise(mean_sbp = mean(BPSys1), 
            n = n())
```

::: {.fragment}
::: {.callout-warning}
`drop_na()` without column names drops rows with **any** NA. 

Check `nrow()` before and after. Which one is the right choice is an explicit **analytic decision**, not just a technicality!
:::
:::

## Does it matter for the answer?

::: {.fragment}
This is a rhetorical question...

```{r}
#| eval: false

# all ages vs. adults only
nh_ghb |> 
  summarise(mean_sbp = mean(BPSys1, na.rm = TRUE))
## vs
nh_ghb |> 
  filter(Age >= 18) |> 
  summarise(mean_sbp = mean(BPSys1, na.rm = TRUE))
```
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.callout-tip title="Challenge"}
Among adults, is `BPSys1` missing more often in one sex or one age group? Or one BMI class? Use `is.na()` inside `group_by() |> summarise()`.
:::

More on missing data might come in a later session!
:::

# 3. Dates

## Dates arrive as text

::: {.fragment}
... and in many cases you have to hope they are formatted right!
:::

::: {.fragment}
```{r}
#| eval: true
linelist <- data.frame(
  id     = 1:6,
  onset  = c("2024-03-01", "2024-03-02", "2024-03-05",
             "2024-03-09", "2024-03-10", "2024-03-12"),
  report = c("2024-03-04", "2024-03-05", "2024-03-07",
             "2024-03-12", "2024-03-15", "2024-03-14")
)

glimpse(linelist)
```
:::

::: {.fragment}
R does not know these are dates (yet) - Your best friend, possibly: `lubridate` (yes, package developers often like word puns)
:::

## Parse them

This is - of course - just an appetizer

::: {.fragment}
```{r}
#| eval: true
#| output-location: fragment

library("lubridate")
linelist <- linelist |>
  mutate(onset = ymd(onset), 
         report = ymd(report))

glimpse(linelist)

dmy("01/03/2024")              # other orders: dmy(), mdy()
ymd("2024-13-45")              # what happens with impossible dates?
```
:::

## Compute with dates

Keeping it simple here...

::: {.fragment}
```{r}
#| eval: true
linelist |>
  mutate(delay = report - onset)               # a time difference

linelist |>
  mutate(delay_days = as.numeric(report - onset)) |>
  summarise(mean_delay = mean(delay_days))
```

... but you can see that some simple functions make this quite easy!
:::

## From dates to weeks

There are clever ways of converting among units!

::: {.fragment}
```{r}
#| eval: true
linelist |>
  mutate(week = floor_date(onset, unit = "week")) 
```
:::

::: {.fragment}
```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
linelist |>
  mutate(week = floor_date(onset, unit = "week")) |>
  count(week) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = week, y = n)) +
  geom_col()
```
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.callout-note}
NHANES has no calendar dates, but outbreak data will be full of them.
:::
:::

# Recap

## Develop (at least) these habits

::: {.incremental}
* Check the **type** of every column (`glimpse()` or `summary()` can be your very good friends)
* Set the **order** of categories on purpose
* Ask **why** something is missing before dealing with it
:::

::: {.fragment}
You are the one wanting to become an epidemiologist, right?

Always remember: to get the right answer, start asking the right question(s) - and don't be afraid to ask questions.
:::
